q: The technician reads you the ground-tackle line of the inventory in the office and offers you the pen. What do you do?
a: Go to the bow first and see the anchor and the chain yourself
o: Sign — the inventory is the base's own record of the boat
Sign, and check the anchor on the first evening at anchor
Ask for a heavier anchor; 25 kg is too light for 45 ft
why: You sign for what you have seen: anchor type and size on the roller, chain in the locker.

q: You ask about the chain marks. 'Every ten metres, you will see them,' says the technician. What do you do?
a: Ask for the colour code and write it on the check-in form
o: Take his word — paint marks are the same across the fleet
Count the marks yourself the first time you anchor
Ask for the chain to be re-marked before departure
why: Scope is laid by the marks; without the code you do not know how much chain is out.

fig.title: Anchor chain
lines: Colour code: not on the form

q: You lift the locker lid and trace the chain to its end. What do you ask for?
a: A rope lashing at the bitter end that you can cut in an emergency
o: A bigger shackle — the last link takes the whole load
Nothing — a shackled end can never be lost overboard
Ten metres of rope spliced on to make the chain longer
why: The bitter end is tied with rope so the whole rode can be cut away if you must leave the anchor fast.

fig.title: Anchor locker
lines: Bitter end: shackled hard to the eye bolt

q: On the foredeck the technician points at the two foot switches and hands you the windlass remote. What do you do before you leave the bow?
a: Run the chain out and in from both switches and from the remote
o: Try the remote only — the foot switches are a backup
Note 'windlass OK' — he has just shown you the controls
Try it on the first anchorage, with a real load on the chain
why: Test every control both ways at the pontoon; a dead 'up' switch is found at the base, not in a bay.

q: During the test the windlass motor hums and runs, but the gypsy does not turn and the chain stays where it is. What do you do?
a: Tighten the clutch with the windlass handle and try again
o: Reset the breaker at the panel and try again
Ask for the windlass motor replaced before departure
Note the windlass as faulty and plan to anchor by hand
why: A slipping clutch: the gypsy is not locked to the shaft. The handle tightens it — and frees it to lower by hand.

q: You press the foot switch and nothing happens. You go below and find the panel like this. What do you do?
a: Switch the windlass breaker on, start the engine and try again
o: Write 'windlass dead' on the check-in form and ask for an electrician
Ask the base to charge the batteries overnight before you test it
Lower the anchor on the clutch to test the chain run instead
why: The windlass has its own breaker and is used with the engine running — its current would flatten the house bank.

q: The technician showed you the snubber at check-in. On your first night you are anchored as drawn and the wind is building. What do you do with the chain?
a: Hook the snubber on, take the load to a cleat and slacken the chain on the gypsy
o: Leave the chain on the gypsy — the windlass brake is made for it
Set the chain stopper and keep the snubber for a real gale
Lead the chain round the mast foot and make it fast there
why: The windlass is not a mooring point: the snubber takes the snatch loads, the chain stopper backs it up.

q: At the bow the technician opens the locker and you see this. He says the shower hose does the chain. What do you do?
a: Ask for the drain cleared and the washdown shown working, and note both
o: Accept the shower hose — it rinses the chain just as well
Accept it — the locker empties itself once you are sailing
Ask for a bucket and bail the locker out once a day
why: Standing water and mud in the locker rot the chain and the boat; the washdown is listed, so it must work.

q: You find the bow roller like this. 'It has been that way all season,' says the technician. What do you do?
a: Photograph it, write it on the check-in form and ask for a pin before you leave
o: Take his word — a season of use shows that it holds
Refuse the boat until the roller is replaced with a new one
Say nothing now and call it pre-existing damage at check-out
why: Damage not on the form is yours at check-out; the pin keeps the anchor from jumping the roller at sea.

q: The technician ticks the second anchor without going aft: 'It is in the lazarette.' What do you do?
a: Ask him to dig it out and show you the anchor, the warp and the shackle together
o: Tick it — a kedge is hardly ever used on a week's charter
Ask for a second all-chain rode in place of the rope warp
Check the warp length only; the anchor is a standard item
why: A kedge without its warp or shackle is no anchor; see the whole kit and where it lives.

q: You anchor for lunch where the figure shows, the way the briefing described. How much chain do you lay, counting the marks?
a: Three marks, 30 m: 4–5 × the 7 m from roller to seabed
o: One mark, 10 m: the chain's own weight holds in F3
Two marks, 20 m: three times the charted depth
Seven marks, 70 m: all of it, nothing held back
why: Med scope with all chain is 4–5 × the depth measured from the bow roller, not the waterline.

q: You read the mooring kit against your week. What do you ask the base for before you sign?
a: Stern lines of at least a boat length, and a long line for taking lines ashore
o: Nothing — the lazy lines take the load, and 10 m reaches any quay
A second pair of springs; stern-to is held by the anchor chain
Only the long line — 10 m stern lines are the standard kit
why: A stern line goes to the quay and back; in a bay or at a quay without lazy lines you need a long line ashore.

q: The technician makes a stern line up on the midships cleat to show you the cleat hitch. The line looks like this. What do you do?
a: Ask for it replaced before departure and note the swap on the form
o: Accept it — a stiff line is a strong line, it has not stretched
Accept it and turn it end for end so the chafe sits inboard
Tape over the worn part and keep that line as a spring only
why: A chafed, hardened line parts in the first Meltemi night; mooring lines are the base's to replace, not yours.

fig.note: Hard, kinked; cover worn through in one place

q: The technician counts the fenders out on the pontoon. What do you do?
a: Ask for the flat one pumped or swapped, and note the torn cover on the form
o: Accept them all — fenders are consumables and the deposit covers them
Ask for all the fenders replaced with new ones for a 45 ft boat
Say nothing — a half-flat fender still works against a quay
why: Count, size and condition go on the form; a flat fender is a scraped hull you will pay for.

q: The passerelle is lying on the coachroof, untied. The technician says you will rig it at the first quay. What do you do?
a: Have him show you the fitting and the lashing, and lash it down before you leave
o: Leave it — a passerelle does not move on a coachroof
Tie it to the guardrail with its own bungee for the passage
Ask for it stowed in the base until you need it at a quay
why: A loose plank goes overboard on the first heel; see how it fits and how it is lashed for a passage.

q: At the quay demonstration the technician hauls the lazy line up bare-handed. You will also pick up buoys in the bays. What do you check is aboard before you sign?
a: Gloves for the slime line and a boat hook that locks when extended
o: A second boat hook and a bucket for the mud off the line
Spare lazy lines of your own for quays that have none
A long lanyard so the lazy line can be tied to the pulpit
why: Lazy lines are slimy and cut hands; the boat hook that does the buoys and lines must lock, not telescope back.

fig.note: Slime line hauled up by hand

q: The dinghy is in the water at the pontoon. The technician goes through it with you and you note this. What do you do?
a: Ask for a plug and the boat's name on the tubes before you sign for it
o: Sign — a missing plug only matters when you tow it
Sign and buy a plug and a marker pen in town
Refuse the dinghy and ask for the deposit reduced
why: No plug means a swamped dinghy; without the boat's name a stolen or drifted tender cannot be returned.

fig.title: Dinghy on the inventory
lines: Boat name: not on the tubes

q: First evening, stern-to on the Lefkas town quay on your 42 ft catamaran. You read this clause again. What do you do with the dinghy?
a: Dinghy up on the davits, lifting lines cleated, cable and padlock on
o: Leave it afloat on its painter — the quay is lit and busy all night
Tie it alongside, outboard on, with the kill cord in your pocket
Tow it tomorrow and padlock it only in the empty bays
why: The dinghy is the first thing stolen and the one thing the deposit does not cover; lift it and lock it every night.

fig.title: Contract — dinghy & outboard
lines: Not covered by the damage waiver
Lifted at night; not towed at sea

q: The technician lifts the outboard onto the dinghy and says it 'runs fine'. What do you do?
a: Start it at the pontoon yourself, in neutral, and pull the kill cord to see it stop
o: Take his word and start it the first time you need to go ashore
Ask him to start it and watch from the pontoon
Check the fuel level only — the engine was serviced over the winter
why: An outboard is tested where help is: it starts, it stops on the cord, and you have seen fuel in the tank.

q: The base manager shows you the plan for Friday. Where and how do you bring the boat back?
a: Stern-to at B on the lazy line, by 17:00 on Friday
o: Stern-to at C on your own anchor, as at a town quay
Alongside at A for fuel, and leave the boat there
On a buoy at D and wait for the base to call you in
why: The base takes the boat back where and how the briefing says: its own berth, the lazy line, no anchor, on time.
